questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{4n}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=0$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{4n}=\frac{x}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}+⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{x}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+⋯.
$$

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2n+1}}{n}.

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(2n+1){x}^{2n}}{n}
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(2n+1){x}^{2n}}{n}.
$$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n!}{x}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the Taylor series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$ 

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot \frac{n!}{(-1)^{n-1}{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)x\cdot n!}{(n+1)!}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{|x|}{n+1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges when $L<1.$  Since $0<1$ for all $x,$ we conclude that 
$R=\infty .$

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(4n-1){(\frac{x}{4})}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$

The radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(4(n+1)-1){(\frac{x}{4})}^{n+1}}{(4n-1){(\frac{x}{4})}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{4n+3}{4n-1}||\frac{x}{4}| \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{|x|}{4} & <1 \\ |x| & <4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is $R=4.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(3x)^{n+1}}{{2}^{n+2}}\cdot \frac{{2}^{n+1}}{(3x)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{3x}{2}| \\  & =\frac{3|x|}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3|x|}{2} & <1 \\ |x| & <\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\sqrt{5(n+1)+2}\,(-4x)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{5n+2}\,(-4x)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\sqrt{5n+7}}{\sqrt{5n+2}}||(-4x)| \\  & =4|x|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}4|x| & <1 \\ |x| & <\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is $R=\frac{1}{4}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the First Few Terms for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
canonical_examples.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by

$$
\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty { {{n}}(x-1)^{n}}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=1$ of $f'(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty { {{n}}(x-1)^{n}} = (x-1) + {2(x-1)^2} + {3(x-1)^3} +\cdots .
$$

To find $f'(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1+0+4(x-1)+9(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+4(x-1)+9(x-1)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the First Few Terms for the Derivative of a Taylor Series

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the General Term for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
canonical_examples.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=3$ is given by

$$
\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{ (x-3)^{n}}{n}
$$

Find $a_n,$ given that

$$
f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217743/assets/af9c822ae7190d9d82dbdd5024b5393a912b0cce5af42f39bcb5d37c3e675283.svg)

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217743/assets/111f8df85bc2af18c21b63b254f6d3b679cb9b3a6a1ce35e9b0e4ef85f96ae07.svg)
We can now write the Taylor series for $f'(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty (x-3)^{n-1}.
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
a_n = (x-3)^{n-1}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Radius of Convergence for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
canonical_examples.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$  about $x=0$ is given by 

$$
\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-3)^{n}\,x^n}{n^3}
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x| <            R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of $f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of $f'(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of $f'(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-3)^{n+1}\,{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{3}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3}}{(-3)^{n}\,{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-3)x\cdot {n}^{3}}{(n+1)^{3}}| \\  & =3|x|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{3}} \\  & =3|x|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}3|x| & <1 \\ |x| & <\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R = \dfrac 1 3.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose the Taylor (Maclaurin) series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by 

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1}
$$

and converges to $f(x)$ for $|x| < R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. How can we calculate the first three non-zero terms of Taylor series for the derivative, $f'(x),$ about $x=0?$

All we need to do is differentiate the Taylor series of $f(x).$ Writing out the first three terms, we get

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1} = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^5}{5} - \cdots.
$$

Now, to find $f'(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})-⋯ \\  & =1-{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

And that's it! The radius of convergence of the Taylor series for $f'(x)$ is $R,$ the same as $f(x).$
